title: Chapter 74 – Contribution and Debt
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The first batch sells in an hour, and the second in half that.

Jian stands at the end of the Pill Hall counter with a tray of twelve green Marrow Wash pills, each the size of a bean, and watches them disappear into the sleeves of outer disciples. There is no shouting. The Sect does not permit it. A boy with a coin purse steps up, lays his stones on the wood, says a number under his breath and takes his pills, and the next boy steps forward before the first has turned away.

"Five stones each," says Steward Gu, to the ledger. "The Hall takes three. The apprentice takes two." He taps the tray. "The Hall also takes a share of the herbs, and a share of the fire, and a small sum for the bench. You will find the arithmetic unfriendly."

"I will find it."

"You have found it already, I think." The steward's eyes flick up and down again. "Twelve pills. Twenty-four stones. Less the herbs. Less the fire. Less the bench." He turns the ledger toward Jian with a stubby finger. "Eleven stones and a half."

Jian looks at the figure.

It is the first money he has held since the Register, and it is the first he has earned by his own hands. Eleven and a half low spirit stones. He could buy four days of meals with it, or a decent knife, or a month's worth of lamp oil. He folds his fingers around the coins and thinks, with a small sour clarity, of the hundred and forty-three points of energy he still lacks, and of the clan at home that has been sending him stones for six weeks.

Eleven and a half. It is not a river. It is a drip.

But it is his.

"Steward."

"Yes?"

"May I post a parcel?"

"You may," says Gu, to his hands, "pay the courier at the Outer Affairs Hall, which charges one stone a day's ride and takes no responsibility for anything it carries. I would add a note." He pauses. "I would add a very short note."

* * *

He writes it that night, by Ma Bao's candle, on a leaf of cheap paper.

Father, Mother. I am well. I have a place at the Pill Hall. Ten stones for the clan, from my first pills. Do not send more. Feng is well. Tell Lin Yue the number was three.

It is eleven lines shorter than the one he wrote the first time. He reads it through, and tears away the last line, and puts it back.

Tell Lin Yue the number was three.

A boy at the far end of the room turns over and mutters. The silent boy, whose name Jian has learned is Lan Tong, sits up on his cot with his knees drawn to his chest and his eyes open and unfocused, as he does most nights. He has never said a word. Jian once left a Breath-Gathering pill under his pillow, and the next morning found it on his own, with a small, careful bite out of the edge and a dry brown leaf folded beside it. He has not worked out what the leaf means.

He folds the paper small, wraps the ten stones in a rag, and sleeps.

The courier takes it at dawn.

* * *

The mission board of the Outer Affairs Hall is a wall.

It is forty paces long, of whitewashed plaster, and covered from floor to rafters in slips of yellow paper pinned with bamboo splinters. Each slip is a task. Each task is a price. The clerks change them at dawn and at dusk, and a crowd of outer disciples stands in front of it all day with their heads tilted back, like pilgrims at a shrine.

Jian goes on the eighth day of his trial, at the first bell, with the list in his head.

Five reagents.

He starts at the left end, with the medicine missions, and works along. Terrace Four, weeding, two points. Valley gate, hauling, three. Nightshade survey, five. The prices are low and the work is dull. He is looking for one word. He finds it at the end of the third row, in a small neat hand.

Earthheart root. Medicine Valley, Terrace Eleven. Escort and harvest. Team of four. Reward: forty points, plus one root to the team leader at cost. Requires: Level 2 herb handling or Overseer's writ.

There. He reads it twice. He does not touch the slip. He moves on.

Beast Mountains edge. Stone-boar cull. Team of four. Reward: eighty points; beast parts to the hunters. Marrow of a second-rank beast available to the team leader by request. The slip has a tiny red mark in the corner, a seal of caution. Rank 2 beast. QR9 or above recommended.

Second-rank. His chest tightens a little. Not at the beast. At the sentence: marrow available to the team leader. There is a road, then. A narrow one.

He finds the rest by walking. At the far end of the wall, behind a plain wooden screen, the clerks have pinned a notice that is not a mission at all. Market Town Auction. Fifteenth of the month. Alchemical materials. Pale jade powder, various grades, expected. Entrance: ten stones. The fifteenth is thirty-five days away.

And at the very end, on a slip of red paper with a seal and a black border, the last two.

Azure dew. Sect Treasury, third vault. Released by writ of an Elder or on requisition by an Inner Sect disciple. Amount: three drops per requisition.

Sun-forged cinnabar. Furnace Peak stores. Released by writ of an Elder or on requisition by an Inner Sect disciple. Amount: two grains per requisition.

He stands in front of the red slips for a long moment.

Both of them. Not one. Both of the restricted pair require the same thing: an Elder's name or an Inner Sect badge. He has neither. He is an Outer Sect disciple of the first rank, twenty years old, with eighty points and eleven stones, and a trial month.

Five reagents, four roads, and two of them closed.

"You are standing in my light," says a voice.

* * *

She has come up on his left, quietly, and she is smiling.

It is not a warm smile. It is the careful, composed, exact smile of someone who has been trained in smiling by people who cared very much about the result. She is seventeen, perhaps, tall and slim, in an outer disciple's gray tunic that has been tailored in a way no outer disciple can afford. A silver comb holds up her hair. A purse at her waist is stitched in blue silk. She carries herself like a person who has never once waited in a line.

"Forgive me," says Jian. "I did not see."

"No. You were reading." Her eyes pass over the red slips and return to him. They are very bright and perfectly polite. "The restricted shelf. A curious thing for a first-year to read."

"I read everything, Senior Sister. It passes the time."

"Does it?" She tilts her head. "You are Lin Jian. From Green Pine Hill. The boy who reads fire and keeps a ledger under his cot." The smile does not change. "People talk in a courtyard. I am Tan Ruyan."

Tan. He knows the name. It is on the second row of the roll in the Register hall, in the column of the first thirty: the daughter of a merchant house in the river city of Qingshi, a Qi Refining eighth layer at the age of seventeen, ranked fourth in the Outer Court.

"I have heard of you, Senior Sister."

"Everyone has. It is tiresome." She steps past him to the board and runs a finger lightly along the row of medicine missions. "I wonder what you want with Azure dew. Or cinnabar. An outer disciple has no use for either."

"I have no use for them, Senior Sister. I was reading."

"Of course." The finger stops on the slip for the Earthheart root. She takes it down, with a practiced little motion, and turns it to the light. "I wonder why you should be looking at Terrace Eleven. It is the sort of mission a person takes who wishes to attempt Foundation." Her gaze lifts to his, unhurried. "It is what I am doing. I have a pill, you see. I have been paying for it since the autumn."

Paying.

"I take it you are in the same line," says Tan Ruyan. "The Pill Hall's boy, who reads fire. I have heard that too." She lays the slip against her palm. "I should tell you before we are surprised by each other. I mean to take the root, and the boar, and everything else on this wall that leads to an Inner Sect badge. I have a head start of six months and a clan that can afford to lose a little. I would be sorry if we collided."

It is, in its way, honest. He finds that he respects it.

"I would be sorry too, Senior Sister."

"Good." She slides the slip into her sleeve, a quick clean movement, and signs her name on the clerk's board with a silver pen. "Then we shall be civil." She inclines her head, exactly the width a disciple of the fourth rank owes to one of the four hundredth, and turns away. "Good morning, Disciple Lin."

He watches her go. She does not hurry. The crowd parts for her in the way crowds part for people who have never needed to ask.

She has taken the root mission. The boar next, I would guess.

The slips are still on the wall. He could take one now. He does not. A boy with eighty points and a trial month cannot put his name to a four-man mission on his own, and every slip on the board needs three companions he has not got.

She did not take the red ones. He turns the thought over. Because she cannot either.

For all her silk and her silver, Tan Ruyan is on the same side of the red line as he is.

* * *

He goes to look at Terrace Eleven the next morning, because a thing seen is a thing priced.

Medicine Valley lies behind the Outer Court on the north side of the mountain, a long green cleft with a stream at the bottom and terraces cut up both slopes like the steps of a giant's stair. The lower terraces are open: servants in brown bend over beds of nightshade and bitterwort, their sleeves rolled to the elbow. Overseer Han walks the path between them with an abacus on his belt and a bamboo pointer in his hand, and every few paces he stops, taps a bed, and says a number.

He is a short, stout, red-faced man with the manner of someone who has been told the terraces are his and intends to be believed.

"Terrace Eleven," he says, when Jian asks. He does not stop walking. "Forty paces above the weeping stone. You will see the gate."

Jian sees the gate. It is an arch of gray stone, small and unremarkable, with two guards in the blue of the Outer Affairs Hall standing on either side. A thin band of yellow light runs along the top of the arch where an array has been drawn into the stone. Behind it, on the slope, a few dozen plants stand in a bed of black earth with a low iron fence around it. They are the height of his knee. They have broad, dull red leaves, and the air above them shimmers very slightly, the way air shimmers over a hot road.

Level 2 herbs. He does not have to scan them. The pressure is there at forty paces: a slow heavy sweetness in his teeth, like the smell of rain on stone.

"Earthheart," says Han, who has stopped, after all, at his elbow. "Four hundred years old, the first plants. Cuttings, since. It grows a root the size of a man's fist in thirty years, and not a day sooner." He taps the bamboo against his palm. "You will have seen the mission."

"I have, Overseer."

"You will have seen Level 2 handling." The red face turns to him. "Do you know what that means?"

"No."

"It means a hand that has made a Level 2 pill. Or a hand that has been taught to pull a Level 2 root by an Elder of this Valley, who will sign a paper." Han's bright, wary eyes rake over Jian. "You are ten. You are Bai's boy. Bai's signature is good here. He has not given one in nineteen years."

"I understand, Overseer."

"Do you? Good." The pointer goes back to his belt. "Then you understand that a twenty-year-old who comes to my gate with a Pill Hall chit and a request for Level 2 roots is a twenty-year-old whom I will remember." A pause. "I am not unkind. I am careful. Terrace Eleven loses one plant in a season to the beasts, and I answer for each. I should like to answer for as few as possible."

"Yes, Overseer."

"Go and look at the weeds. They are cheaper."

He goes. At the bottom of the path, he stops and turns, and looks back at the bed of red leaves on the slope, the faint shimmer, the two guards. He imagines it with four people on it, in the dusk, with a knife, and a sack, and a boy who does not know what his Seal will do in the presence of that much old Earth Qi.

It would answer, he thinks. The root. I would not be able to keep it quiet.

* * *

He trains at dawn on the following mornings, on Terrace Nine, before the bell.

There is no one to see. The terrace is a long grassy shelf above the moonroot beds, with a few old pines at the back and a view down the valley to the roofs of the Court. The light comes gray and cold. He takes off his sandals and stands on the damp earth with his feet apart and begins the form.

It is not a sect form. He does not know any sect forms. It is the Seasons Veil, which Qinghe taught him in the Garden's shadow, and the slow Wheel beneath it. He lets the false cycle turn, spring to summer, summer to autumn, autumn to winter, and under the false cycle he lets the true one move at half its pace. Hiding is not a thing one does once. It is a thing one does at every breath.

Three layers. I am a boy of the third layer.

The Veil holds, as long as he does not think about it.

He puts his hand on the hilt of Mu's blade, which hangs at his belt in a plain sheath, and it is a Pool-grade key, and he does not draw it. He draws instead the pins. Six of them, no longer than a finger, from the roll of cloth in his sleeve. He tests the weight of each on his palm.

He has twelve more at home. He has spent nearly all his stones on reagents. These six cost him a morning of Fabrication and a nosebleed, and he intends to keep them.

He throws them at a knot in the nearest pine.

They go in a line, one after another, at a distance of eleven paces. Four stick, two bounce. He walks up, recovers them, wipes the sap with his thumb and walks back. He does it again. He does it again. After the ninth round, all six stick in a palm-wide circle, and he stands with his arms at his sides and his breath white in the cold air and feels, in his shoulders, the dull steady ache of work that has been done correctly.

Better. Not good.

A bird cries in the pines. The valley lights with the first thin gold. Below him, across the roofs, the bell of the Contribution Hall tolls the dawn.

He goes down to the day.

* * *

He works that afternoon in the Pill Hall yard with a plan, and a pencil of charcoal, and a bowl of ink.

He cannot do it on the bark. A bark ledger is for sums, and what he needs now is a map. He takes a clean leaf of the cheap paper Gu uses for labels and draws five circles in a row, and next to each circle a word, and below each word the things that stand between him and it.

Root. Medicine Valley, Terrace Eleven. Needs: team of four, an Overseer's writ or Level 2 handling.

Marrow. Beast Mountains edge. Needs: team of four, a team leader's request. Danger: second-rank beast.

Powder. Market Town auction, day fifteen. Needs: stones, perhaps a hundred.

Dew. Sect Treasury. Needs: Elder's writ or Inner Sect rank.

Cinnabar. Furnace Peak. Same.

He draws a line under it. Under the line he writes the last item, in smaller marks, with a care that borders on dread.

Energy: 143.

He does not know how it is to be earned.

That, more than the board or the rival or the red slips, is the thing that sits cold in his stomach. The Interface does not pay by labor. It pays in a currency of its own, for the things it deems of value: a marked enemy removed, a mystery opened, a task completed to its own accounting. In the Garden, at the Siege, at Red Ridge, the rewards came in lumps of twenty, sixty, a hundred and thirty. He has never planned for them. He has simply survived and found the panel waiting.

It is not a wage. It is a tide.

He rereads the Interface's own wording, carefully, from memory. Removal of a bound agent. The Level 3 Separation of living tissue and bound agents, he knows, is an ability, not a source. But the last time he had cut something loose, at the Garden's gate, the panel had paid. The hook in Feng's heel, the thread in Heng's throat, the mark under the watcher's tongue: they are all the same kind of thing. They are things that have been bound to a living person by someone else.

Bound agents.

He stares at the phrase for a long time.

If there is a tide, he thinks, it is flowing toward the Blood Shadow. They have bound a great many people. Every thread removed, every hook severed, might be worth something to a system that counts such things. But every thread removed also means standing next to a Blood Shadow's work, and he has seen what happens when a question is asked of a marked man.

And I cannot Scan. I have seven.

He turns to the second page of the plan, the one that has no circles, only names.

Team of four. A mission needs a leader and three hands, and every hand is a person who will see what Jian does. Feng is the obvious first. He is QR9, the best fighter in the Court, and he has already decided to ask no questions. But Feng's leg gives out at the fourth breath of a hard push, and a mission on the Beast Mountains edge is not a place for a man who may kneel.

Ma Bao is willing and loud, which is a different thing from useful. Pei says the name of a river in his sleep and cannot hold a sword. Lan Tong has not spoken in two months.

And there is the boy from Red Ridge, Zhao Yao, whom Jian has seen across the Hundred Stairs twice, watching him with the careful still attention of a person who has not decided what he is looking at. A cousin of the man in the cold cells. A boy whose clan Jian has taken apart, stone by stone.

Not him. Not yet. He writes the name anyway, and draws a small circle around it, and puts a question mark inside.

He folds the paper and puts it in his sleeve.

* * *

The note arrives that evening.

A servant brings it to the courtyard at the hour of the gong, a boy in brown with a blank face, and puts it in Jian's hand without a word. It is a small square of gray paper, folded twice. There is no seal. There is a smell of iron.

The new moon is tomorrow night.

The offer stands. A seedling from the Garden, in a pot, before the third watch. In return: my introduction to an Elder of the Inner Sect, a writ for the dew, and the protection of the Contribution Hall for the length of your trial. No one need know.

I am a patient man. I would not wish the Court to learn about your moonroot, or about the other matter.

There is no signature. There is no need. The hand is the hand that wrote the register, a fine, flat, upright script that he has seen on his own account page, and the last line is underlined once, very lightly, in a faint brown ink.

The other matter.

He does not move. A cold, clear sensation moves through him, like water poured down a spine. The other matter. The Deacon cannot mean the Garden. The Garden is held in trust by the Court, by a decree he has read. He cannot mean the cradle; no one knows of it but Jian. He cannot mean Pebble, who has been registered at the Beast Hall.

He means the scan. He means the smell of copper. He means whatever he saw in my face when I read his page.

Or he means nothing, and is guessing.

That is what a threat is. A guess that you cannot afford to test.

Jian sits on the edge of his cot with the paper in his hand and the courtyard going quiet around him. Ma Bao has begun to snore. Pei, who has been talking in his sleep for a week, says the name of a river. The lamp gutters.

He lays out the choice, as he has learned to, in a column.

Accept. A seedling is a cutting from the Garden, a living thing, a trade. But the Garden is the clan's. It is held in trust, and a seedling of the Five Seasons in the hands of a Blood Shadow impostor is a seedling that can be copied, studied, perhaps used to find the beds. The Deacon has told him so himself, by asking for it.

And the introduction. An Elder of the Inner Sect, a writ for the dew. That is the door he cannot open for himself. It is, he thinks, exactly why the Deacon has named it.

Refuse. He keeps the Garden. He keeps his name. He keeps, he supposes, his own honor, and loses the one road that would take him quickly to the red slips. And the Deacon, who is not merely a Deacon, who writes in iron-ink and bleeds it through glass, learns that the boy cannot be bought and knows too much.

Delay. He considers that for some time. A delay is a refusal that has not been admitted. The Deacon would accept it for exactly as long as it suited him.

The column has three lines, and each line ends in the same place.

He will move against me either way.

Jian sets the paper on his knee and looks at it for a long time. Then he takes up the charcoal, turns the paper over, and writes on the back, in his small cramped hand, the thing he has been trying not to write since the glass.

He knows I know.

Across the room, on his cot with his knees drawn up, Lan Tong has turned his head. His dark eyes are on the paper. He does not look away when Jian meets them. He raises one hand, slowly, and lays a dry brown leaf, folded in four, on the blanket between them.

Then he lies down, and turns to the wall, and does not move again.
